catalog_quote: Khumi syllable canon can be characterized as in (6): (6) (C(v))C(C)V(N)+tone Syllables have an underlying tone. The only possible final consonant (with the exceptions discussed earlier) is ng. The first (optional) C(v) portion of the schema in (6) represents the half-syllable found in sesquisyllabic forms. ... no vowel is written in the half syllable: p'liwng4 [pə1liwŋ4] 'heart'. ... Compounding is fairly standard for this part of the world. In Khumi, two-member compounds are typically right-headed (if endocentric) and are phonologically distinguished by the treatment of their first (and sometimes second) element. There are various possibilities, but typically, the first element bears less stress than the second and does not show the full array of tonal distinctions found on its last syllable compared to non-compound occurrences of that member; tonal distinctions on the last syllable of the first member are generally reduced to high vs. low, although tone 4 (rising) in compounds sometimes shows a peak delay that bleeds over into a following syllable, altering the tone of that syllable: e.g., kno4+kho4.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khumi is a tone language (five lexical tones; every syllable carries an underlying tone; syllable canon (C(v))C(C)V(N)+tone with toneless/reduced half-syllables in sesquisyllables). The only stress statement located is at compound level: in a two-member compound the second (head) member is the more stressed one and the first member is weaker, with its tones neutralised to a high/low contrast. No rule for stress placement in simple words was found in any snippet or open paper.
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are various possibilities, but typically..' - the first-element reduction is the typical, not the only, pattern; rising tone 4 on a first member can spread its peak into the following syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Compound (two-member) domain, not word or phrase; half-syllables of sesquisyllabic words are written without a vowel and transcribed with a reduced vowel (p'liwng4 [pə1liwŋ4] 'heart'), i.e. the major syllable is the tone-bearing one, but the source is not quoted as calling this stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All Peterson sources describe Bangladesh Khumi (Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bandarban; Peterson 2002 says two mutually intelligible dialects, c. 2,000 speakers at the time), which is the ISO 639-3 cnk / khum1248 variety; Myanmar (Paletwa) Khumi is also cnk. Eastern Khumi Chin [cek] = east2779 is a separate Glottolog language, and the Lemi (Herr 2011) and 'Kanise Khumi' (Tan 2022) theses noted in the earlier scan belong there or need checking; Mro-Khimi [cmr] (Horney 2012) is a different language again. The earlier scan's citation of a Peterson 'Bangladesh Khumi' chapter in Thurgood & LaPolla (2nd ed.) is wrong: Peterson's chapter there is 'Hakha Lai'; the Khumi chapter is in Vittrant & Watkins 2019 (De Gruyter), pp. 12-55.

new_statements.quote: It may here be remarked that, as an almost invariable rule, words of two or three syllables are accented on the last. Hence it will generally be found unnecessary in these notes to indicate accent by any distinguishing mark. [...] * This vowel sound is similar to that of u in but, yet always unaccented.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent falls on the last syllable of di- and trisyllabic words almost without exception; the reduced (schwa-like) presyllable vowel is never accented. Consistent with So-Hartmann 2001:136-137 (Mro ka- 'an unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable') and Hornéy 2012:39 (minor-syllable vowel 'much shorter duration'), i.e. iambic sesquisyllabic prominence on the major/root syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost invariable rule' -- exceptions implied but none listed. Footnote p.219: the reduced vowel 'a as in apology' (the minor-syllable schwa) is 'always unaccented'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from a missionary sketch and spelling-book/reader data (wordlist and sentences); the rule is stated for polysyllabic words generally, including prefixed verbs (ta-, a-, ma- 'frequently occurring prefixes to verbs', p.224). The language is tonal per Hornéy 2012 (H/L, root melodies), which Stilson does not mark or mention; 'accent' here is impressionistic 19th-century stress-accent.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from Stilson 1866 on 'Kemi', the Khami of the northern Arakan plains ('not found farther south than about twenty miles north of Akyab', distinct from the 'Koomis'), data collected 1841-42. ISO 639-3 CR 2011-037 identifies the Arakan-plains 'Awa Khami' with the Wakung sub-group of Mro-Khimi [cmr] (Kyauktaw, Buthidaung, Mrauk-U, Ponnagyun), and Lotven 2021/2023 explicitly equates Stilson's Kemi with Mro-Khimi; the ex-code Khumi Awa [cka] (Glottolog khum1250, now merged) is the same variety. Identity with mroc1235 therefore rests on geography plus Lotven's equation, not on a lexical match; Stilson's 'woman' nāuṅ-pūi-dī ~ Hornéy Wakun /nɛ́pýdí/ but the same root exists in Kanise Khumi. Shafer 1944 'Khimi' is Khumi proper (khum1248), not this language. The modern primary phonology (Hornéy 2012, Wakun dialect) is silent on stress; So-Hartmann 2001 (Wakung) gives only the implicit 'unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable' for ka-.

tone_statements.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2023. Tone in South Central Tibeto-Burman. Himalayan Linguistics 22(1), sec. 2 (and Lotven 2021 PhD diss., Indiana, sec. 6.2).
tone_statements.quote: Peterson (2014, 2019) points out several relevant phonological processes in Khumi that affect the realization of tone. In his analysis, short syllables are considered monomoraic (CV) with one mora, while long syllables are considered bimoraic (CVV), with two moras. ... a mora may be underlyingly [+/- High]. Thus, logical possibilities for tone on a syllable include CV, CV́, CVV, CV́V, CVV́ ... Monomoraic CV and CV́ are faithfully realized as L and H checked pitches (Lʔ, Hʔ), while bimoraic CVV, CV́V, and CVV́ are faithfully realized as L, HL, and LH pitches, respectively.
tone_statements.locator: p. 41, sec. 3.3 'Case study: Khumi'; Table 2 'Underlying contrasts and surface pitch patterns in Khumi (Peterson 2019)' on p. 42; fn. 10 p. 39 lists the 12 surface pitch patterns
tone_statements.summary: Secondhand from Peterson: [+/-High] per mora; five underlying syllable contrasts CV, CV́, CVV, CV́V, CVV́ = Lʔ, Hʔ, L, HL, LH (HL/LH = mora sequences surfacing as fall/rise); 12 surface pitch patterns (fn. 10) via H-deletion, H-retraction, peak delay and grammar. No Khumi words; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.quote: Khumi orthographic double vowels are designed to indicate a three-way tonal contrast: aa (Low tone), áa (High Falling tone) aá (Rising tone). Phonetically Khumi R tone sounds like Rising-Falling. ... such Khumi closed syllables have two tones, namely high short tone (Hs, marked as á) and low short tone (Ls, unmarked as a). ... Khumi also has three tones in smooth syllables (High, Falling, Rising) and two contrastive checked (“short”) tones42, High-checked (“Hc”) and Low-checked (“Lc”). Note that Khumi Hc and Lc tones are sometimes secondary.

Data from Peterson; p. 57: PKC tones only provisionally reconstructible. No stress.

tone_statements.citation: Löffler, Lorenz G. 1960. Khami/Khumi-Vokabulare: Vorstudie zu einer sprachwissenschaftlichen Untersuchung. Anthropos 55(3/4): 505-557.
tone_statements.quote: Daran, daß sowohl Areng als auch Awa (einschließlich Rengmitca) Tonsprachen sind, besteht kein Zweifel ... 1. Mru, Rengmitca, Khumi, Khyang und Born sind Tonsprachen ... 2. Der Tonakzent ist fester Bestandteil einer Silbe ... 3. Es gibt drei Grundtöne mit je zwei Varianten : einer frei ausklingenden und einer durch Glottisverschluß begrenzten Variante. ... 5. Die drei Grundtöne und ihre Varianten sind (dargestellt am Vokal a) : I. ā(k)≷á' : flach oder steigend-kurz II. à(k)≷ā' : fallend oder flach-kurz III. á(k)≷à' : steigend oder fallend-kurz
tone_statements.translation: There is no doubt that both Areng and Awa (including Rengmitca) are tone languages ... 1. Mru, Rengmitca, Khumi, Khyang and Born are tone languages ... 2. The tonal accent is a fixed component of a syllable ... 3. There are three basic tones, each with two variants: one dying away freely and one bounded by a glottal stop. ... 5. The three basic tones and their variants are (shown on the vowel a): I. ā(k)≷á': level, or rising-short; II. à(k)≷ā': falling, or level-short; III. á(k)≷à': rising, or falling-short.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4 'Das Tonsystem', pp. 519-521; tone list item 5 on p. 521
tone_statements.summary: Three basic syllable tones (level, falling, rising), each with an open and a glottal-checked short variant, partly interchangeable; stop-final syllables also bear one of them. Author calls it preliminary; word list marks tone only where fairly certain (not counted). Stress: reduced presyllables.
